channel.title: Learn to Code on Pandaqi Tutorials
channel.description: Recent content in Learn to Code on Pandaqi Tutorials

item.title: Introduction
item.description: You want to learn how to program. Smart! Programming is a job in high demand, with a high salary and many opportunities. Or maybe it’s just a hobby, a skill you’d like to understand. Or maybe you like gaming and want to create your own games.

item.title: Solving Puzzles
item.description:
You have something you want to do. A problem to solve—or a puzzle, that sounds more fun.

Say you’re making a game. You want the character to jump when the player presses spacebar. It won’t happen magically. Hey, that’s a puzzle we need to solve!

item.title: Data Types
item.description: Data types will always be your first step into any programming language—or any problem. That’s not surprising: you already know that coding is just “changing data”. So it obviously all starts with data! Pieces of information of a certain type.

item.title: Variables
item.description: Alright, you can now define data (bool, number, string) and do some calculations. But once you have your result, you want to store it somewhere. You want to put your data on a shelf with a clear label that says what’s inside. Otherwise, you’d have to redo the whole calculation every time!

item.title: Variables II: Naming
item.description: Previous chapter introduced you to the wonderful world of giving names to everything. But can you use any name for your variable? The answer is no, but it’s close.

item.title: Conditionals I
item.description: What you’ve learned so far is already very powerful. Hopefully you’ve played around with the examples, tried writing your own little programs. Calculate something, store it, output it. Exactly the steps in our “problem solving” loop from the beginning.

item.title: Conditionals II
item.description: Last chapter introduced turning everything into a bool. And then using that to determine if we want to execute a group of code or not.

item.title: Numbers
item.description: This chapter is probably most fun if we use an example throughout. (Otherwise, numbers easily become abstract and, well, boring.) Many courses leave chapters like this for last—or leave them out entirely.

item.title: Strings
item.description: String transformations are more fun and specific than the ones for numbers. But they are also more varied, with a huge number of possible things you might want to do.

item.title: Comments & Space
item.description: Human language uses a lot of space. We put a space between every word! We put space around text in a book. Because if it’s pushed against the edge of the paper, it looks ugly and unreadable.

item.title: Loops I
item.description: A crucial principle in programming is “DRY”: Don’t Repeat Yourself. That’s the beauty of a computer: it doesn’t mind executing the same task 1000 times for you. In a sense, that’s all programming is. You give a computer a pattern it can repeat as much as you want.

item.title: Loops II
item.description: Last chapter introduced you to loops. It also teased a different way to play with how many (or which) iterations are executed. Let’s dive into that here.

item.title: Bags I
item.description: Loops really start to shine when you combine it with repeated data: a bag full of values. They’re like twins. A loop repeats code, the bag provides a new element every iteration.

item.title: Bags II
item.description: Last chapter teased the idea of naming the elements inside your bag. Like we give names to things in the real world. Or like putting a label / tag on it.

item.title: Bags III
item.description: What can we do so far? We can define a bag and get what’s inside. But that’s not all you can do with a bag. We’d also like to add new things to it, or remove things from it.

item.title: Machines I
item.description: Congratulations! You’ve arrived at the final boss of programming. Not necessarily because it’s hard, but because it’s the most important and powerful tool.

item.title: Machines II
item.description: You’ve learned how to define (or “create”) a machine and how to tell it to do something. But just like our coffee machine needs beans to create coffee, most machines you write will need some input.

item.title: Machines III
item.description: As you know by now, I am fond of recreating functionality yourself. Even if a language supports something (with an easy keyword), I think it’s a great exercise to try and code it yourself.

item.title: Machines IV
item.description: This is the last chapter with exercises / examples for machines. As you noticed, machines get more chapters than any other topic! This reflects how important they are. How, in the end, all your programs will be built from many tiny machines that do one specific thing.

item.title: Debugging
item.description: Here’s a secret. As a programmer, you actually don’t spend most of your time programming. Instead, most of the time you are reading or fixing code in a process called debugging.

item.title: Data Manipulation I
item.description: In these two chapters, I want to give a few slightly more “advanced” ways for manipulating data. Again, every programming language will have these. And you will use them a lot.

item.title: Data Manipulation II
item.description: In the Strings chapter, I promised some more “bag-like” operations to do on strings. They can be extremely important or not important at all, depending on your project. Still, all languages support them, and I wanted to end the course with these.

item.title: Where to go now?
item.description:
Well done! You’ve read and worked through the whole course. The hard part is over.

Why? Because any language you’ll use in the future will have the things I mentioned. They might change the name, or the symbol, or some detail.

item.title: Conclusion
item.description:
This concludes the course about learning to code.

Hopefully, I was able to ignite a spark. That’s why I learned to code, so long ago. The idea that I could make my own game or website, that I could let the computer solve problems for me, felt like magic. It still feels like magic, sometimes. Honestly, often my code works and I don’t even know why 😛
